title: The Stale Dashboard

scenario.situation: The cached metrics layer serves dashboards in ~80ms but occasionally surfaces stale numbers. Executives have started double-checking figures manually, eroding trust in the platform.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The engineering team wants to remove the cache entirely and query the warehouse directly on every request to guarantee correctness.
scenario.question: Is removing the cache the right fix for the staleness problem?

decisions.prompt: The team is ready to rip out the cache. How do you frame the investigation before any changes are made?

options.label: Plan the cache removal migration
options.detail: Accept the team's diagnosis and focus on how to remove the cache with minimal downtime.
options.consequence: You start planning the migration and quickly find warehouse query costs and p95 latency projections are alarming — but you're already anchored on removal as the solution and the team resists backtracking.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the team's proposed fix before diagnosing whether the fix matched the actual problem.

options.label: Diagnostic counterfactual: model the no-cache world first
options.detail: Before touching anything, simulate what removing the cache costs (latency, warehouse spend) AND audit which specific metrics are actually going stale and how often.
options.consequence: You map two things simultaneously: the staleness incidents cluster on a handful of high-volatility metrics, and the projected no-cache cost is 8–12x higher with p95 latency jumping to ~4 seconds. The removal path is now clearly disproportionate.

options.label: Survey executives about which numbers they distrust
options.detail: Interview stakeholders to build a list of metrics they find unreliable.
options.consequence: Executives flag a long list of metrics — mostly because distrust is now general, not because all metrics are actually stale. You end up over-indexing on perception rather than measured staleness frequency.
options.divergenceCost: Used a perception-biased instrument instead of measured staleness data, inflating the apparent scope of the problem.

options.label: Set a universal shorter TTL on the cache
options.detail: Halve the TTL for all cached metrics to reduce staleness windows across the board.
options.consequence: Staleness incidents drop modestly, but warehouse query volume doubles and costs spike. You've applied a blunt instrument without knowing which metrics actually need fresher data.
options.divergenceCost: Jumped to a blanket parameter change without segmenting metrics by volatility — traded one problem for another.

decisions.prompt: You audit the last 90 days of staleness incidents. Which view of the data do you trust to identify where the real problem lives?

artifact.title: Staleness incidents by metric category — last 90 days (raw count)
artifact.caption: Raw incident counts look spread across several categories. But some categories contain far more individual metrics than others — is the risk actually uniform?

options.label: Raw staleness incident count per metric category
options.detail: Use the absolute number of staleness incidents per category to rank problem areas.
options.consequence: Revenue and Active Users look equally problematic to Real-time event counts — but Revenue has 60 metrics in its category while Real-time event counts has only 4. You're reading category size, not per-metric staleness risk.
options.divergenceCost: Compared raw counts across categories with different numbers of metrics — a denominator blind spot.

options.label: Staleness rate per metric (incidents ÷ metrics in category), cross-referenced with update frequency
options.detail: Normalize incidents by the number of metrics in each category, then tag each category by how frequently its underlying data actually changes.
options.consequence: Normalized and cross-referenced, the picture is unmistakable: Real-time event counts has a staleness rate 6x higher than any other category AND updates every few seconds — the current TTL is wildly mismatched. Revenue and cost metrics update daily and their normalized rate is near zero. The fix is targeted, not global.

artifact.title: Staleness rate per metric × update volatility (normalized)
artifact.caption: Normalized to metrics-per-category, real-time event counts are an outlier — 8.8 incidents per metric vs. ≤1.4 everywhere else. These 4 metrics drive the majority of executive distrust and are the only ones needing event-driven invalidation.

decisions.prompt: The normalized data shows staleness is overwhelmingly concentrated in a small set of high-volatility metrics. What do you tell the engineering team?

options.label: "The cache is fine — just add event-driven invalidation for real-time metrics and close the ticket."
options.detail: Make the prescriptive call directly and implement the fix.
options.consequence: You ship event-driven invalidation for the four outlier metrics and staleness incidents drop. But you haven't validated the TTL settings on the remaining categories or confirmed that the invalidation logic handles backpressure — a busy event stream could thrash the cache in production.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed completeness of the fix without stress-testing the invalidation approach or reviewing TTLs on remaining categories.

options.label: "Removing the cache is disproportionate — staleness concentrates in ~4 high-volatility metrics. The evidence points to event-driven invalidation for those plus a TTL audit for the rest. We should validate in staging before rolling out."
options.detail: Present the finding, flag what's still uncertain, and recommend a staged confirmation path.
options.consequence: The team sees the cost/latency counterfactual, understands the fix is surgical not global, and agrees to a staging validation. The TTL audit surfaces two more misconfigured categories. Trust in the dashboard recovers without a costly cache removal.

insight: Staleness was real but highly concentrated — four real-time event metrics accounted for the majority of incidents while dozens of low-volatility metrics had near-zero staleness rates. Removing the cache would have multiplied costs and latency by an order of magnitude to solve a problem that only required event-driven invalidation on a handful of metrics and a per-category TTL audit. The lesson: match cache freshness to each metric's actual update volatility, and always model the counterfactual cost before accepting a stakeholder's proposed fix as the frame for your investigation.
